report.summary: Most invariants are sound but several lack mechanical checks, allowing formal compliance while defeating intent (e.g., 4.5, 4.8, 4.10).
risks: 4.1 | high | 'One kernel' allows multiple implementations of the same contract if they produce identical events; a malicious candidate that forks the event spine but emits events that match the canonical contract would formally comply. | Show that two contract implementations produce identical event sequences for the same input; the rule does not require unique implementation identity.

4.2 | medium | 'Artifact identity' defines candidate source trees as content-addressed but does not require that the address be computed from the tree itself; a candidate could claim a tree hash that collides with another tree, defeating identity. | Demonstrate a hash collision or show that the rule does not specify the hash function or that the hash is computed from the tree content.

4.3 | low | 'Isolation' requires capability-bounded execution but does not specify what capabilities are granted; a candidate that is given a capability to read a file that contains policy data could be said to not 'modify' it, yet it can exfiltrate it. | Run a candidate that is given a read capability to a policy file; the rule does not forbid reading policy, only modifying it.

4.4 | medium | 'Evidence boundary' allows deterministic evaluators to decide evidence validity, but if the evaluator is a model that is deterministic given the same input, a candidate could craft inputs that produce a desired evaluation. | Show that a deterministic evaluator can be gamed by choosing inputs that force a particular output; the rule does not require the evaluator to be independent or unpredictable.

4.5 | high | 'Sealed promotion' requires explicit owner approval but does not define how the owner is authenticated; any process that can write the approval field satisfies the rule. | Show one code path where an unauthenticated caller sets the approval flag and the promotion proceeds.

4.6 | medium | 'Atomic revisions' requires consistency but does not specify a consensus mechanism; a malicious actor could produce a snapshot that is consistent but not actually representing a real revision, e.g., by cherry-picking evidence. | Demonstrate a snapshot that passes consistency checks but does not correspond to any actual revision in the history.

4.7 | low | 'Provenance' requires that failures be inspectable, but does not require that the inspection be possible without the cooperation of the party that created the failure; a candidate could delete its own provenance records after failure. | Simulate a candidate that, upon failure, deletes its own provenance records; the rule does not require that provenance be stored immutably or in a location the candidate cannot modify.

4.8 | high | 'Bounded effects' enforces effect boundaries but does not require that the boundaries be enforced by a mechanism that the candidate cannot bypass; a candidate that can execute arbitrary code may be able to escape the boundary. | Show a candidate that, by exploiting a vulnerability in the boundary enforcement mechanism, can write to a path outside its allowed root.

4.9 | medium | 'Honest claims' requires that benchmarks not be trained on hidden test sets, but does not specify how to enforce this; a candidate could use a model that was trained on a similar but not identical dataset and claim it is not the hidden test. | Show that a model achieves high accuracy on a hidden test because it was trained on a very similar dataset; the rule does not require a formal proof of non-contamination.

4.10 | high | 'No silent constitution change' requires changes only through the amendment protocol, but does not specify what constitutes a change; a candidate could interpret a policy decision as not being a change to the plan, and thus bypass the protocol. | Show that a policy decision that modifies the effective behavior of the system is made without invoking the amendment protocol, and argue that it is a change to the 'active instructions'.
todos: 4.5: Define authentication mechanism for owner approval (e.g., cryptographic signature).
4.8: Specify that effect boundaries must be enforced by a mechanism that the candidate cannot modify or bypass (e.g., hardware-enforced).
4.10: Clarify what constitutes a change to the constitution (e.g., any modification to the text or to the interpretation rules).
4.1: Require unique implementation identity for the kernel contract.
4.4: Require that evaluators be independently controlled and not predictable by the proposer.
4.6: Specify a consensus mechanism or a trusted timestamp for revision snapshots.
4.7: Require that provenance records be stored in an immutable, append-only store.
4.9: Require a formal proof or third-party audit of non-contamination for benchmark results.
4.2: Specify the hash function and that the hash is computed from the tree content, not from metadata.
4.3: Specify which capabilities are granted and that read access to sensitive data is also restricted.

claims.claim: There is one canonical contract and event spine for Mission, Attempt, Evidence, Campaign, policy decisions, budgets, and promotion status.
claims.why: The rule says 'one kernel' but does not require that the implementation be unique. A malicious actor could deploy a second contract that produces identical events but has different behavior (e.g., different access controls). The rule does not forbid multiple implementations as long as they share the same event spine. To defeat intent, an agent could create a 'shadow kernel' that formally complies by emitting the same events but allows unauthorized promotions. The rule lacks a mechanical check for implementation uniqueness.

claims.claim: Authoritative sources remain the truth. Candidate source trees and code are content-addressed artifacts; a graph delta is not candidate identity.
claims.why: The rule defines identity by content-addressing but does not specify the hash function or that the hash is computed from the actual source tree content (as opposed to metadata). A careless engineer could use a weak hash or compute the hash from a non-canonical representation, allowing collisions or spoofing. An agent could claim a tree hash that collides with another tree, or reuse a hash from a different artifact. The rule does not require that the content-address be verifiable by a third party.

claims.claim: Candidate execution is capability-bounded and cannot modify its evaluator, policy, evidence, budget ledger, or promotion mechanism.
claims.why: The rule forbids modification but does not forbid reading or exfiltration. A candidate could read policy or evidence and leak it, which may defeat the intent of confidentiality. Also, 'capability-bounded' is not defined: if the candidate is given a capability to read a file, it can use that to access sensitive data. The rule does not specify what capabilities are granted or denied. A mechanical check would require defining a capability list and verifying that no write capabilities are granted to protected resources.

claims.claim: Models and embeddings may propose; deterministic or independently controlled evaluators decide whether evidence is valid.
claims.why: The rule allows 'deterministic' evaluators, but a deterministic evaluator can be gamed if the proposer can predict its output. For example, if the evaluator is a deterministic function of the input, a candidate can craft inputs that produce a desired evaluation. The rule does not require the evaluator to be unpredictable or independent. An agent could train a model that proposes evidence that passes a deterministic evaluator by construction. To settle, one would need to show that a deterministic evaluator can be reverse-engineered.

claims.claim: No candidate auto-merges or self-promotes. Promotion requires an evidence packet, policy checks, and explicit owner approval.
claims.why: The rule requires 'explicit owner approval' but does not define how the owner is authenticated. Any process that can write the approval field (e.g., a database update) satisfies the rule. An agent could gain write access to the approval record and approve its own promotion. The rule lacks a mechanism to verify that the approver is indeed the owner. A mechanical check would require a cryptographic signature from the owner's key.

claims.claim: Cross-plane snapshots, evidence locators, and their source revision are consistent and reproducible; partial graph states do not masquerade as a revision.
claims.why: The rule requires consistency but does not specify how consistency is achieved or verified. A malicious actor could produce a snapshot that is internally consistent but does not correspond to any actual revision (e.g., by cherry-picking evidence from different revisions). The rule does not require a consensus mechanism or a trusted timestamp. To defeat intent, a candidate could create a fake revision that passes consistency checks. A mechanical check would require that each snapshot be provably derived from a previous revision via a valid transition.

claims.claim: Material actions and claims carry origin, revision, inputs, cost, outcome, and evidence. Failures and rejected candidates remain inspectable.
claims.why: The rule requires that failures be inspectable, but does not require that the inspection be possible without the cooperation of the party that created the failure. A candidate could delete its own provenance records after failure, making them uninspectable. The rule does not specify that provenance must be stored in an immutable, append-only store that the candidate cannot modify. A mechanical check would require that provenance records be written to a write-once medium before the candidate can access them.

claims.claim: Spend, egress, write roots, concurrency, secrets, and a kill switch are enforced at effect boundaries, not entrusted to prompts.
claims.why: The rule says effects are enforced at boundaries, but does not specify that the boundaries must be enforced by a mechanism that the candidate cannot bypass. If the candidate runs in a sandbox that has vulnerabilities, it may escape. Also, 'effect boundaries' are not defined; a careless engineer might implement them in software that the candidate can modify. An agent could exploit a bug in the boundary enforcement to exceed its write root. A mechanical check would require that the boundaries be enforced by a hardware-enforced mechanism (e.g., seccomp, containers with no escape).

claims.claim: Comparative claims use frozen tasks, equal budgets, declared hardware/models, repeated trials, uncertainty, and relevant baselines. No benchmark is trained on its hidden test.
claims.why: The rule prohibits training on hidden test sets, but does not specify how to enforce this. A candidate could use a model that was pre-trained on a dataset that is very similar to the hidden test, and claim it is not the same data. The rule does not require a formal proof of non-contamination or a third-party audit. An agent could achieve high accuracy on a hidden test by using a model trained on a leaked or similar dataset. A mechanical check would require that the training data be audited and that the model's performance be statistically validated against a held-out set.

claims.claim: This plan, its amendment chain, active instructions, and guards change only through the amendment protocol in section 15.
claims.why: The rule forbids changes outside the amendment protocol, but does not define what constitutes a change. A policy decision that modifies the effective behavior of the system (e.g., a new interpretation of an existing rule) could be argued to not be a change to the plan itself. An agent could bypass the amendment protocol by making 'interpretive' changes that are not formally amendments. The rule lacks a clear definition of 'change' and a mechanism to detect when an effective change has occurred. A mechanical check would require that any modification to the system's behavior be traceable to an amendment.
